REPLY BRIEF OF INTERVENOR JUDY GRACI 
I. INTRODUCTION
Judy Graci, Pro se intervenor submits this Reply Brief in response to the Applicants’ Initial Post-Hearing Brief filed June 19, 2026. The Applicants’ Brief advances five principal arguments in support of need: (1) ERCOT’s recommendation is entitled to “great weight” and effectively resolves the need question; (2) House Bill 5066 authorized the officer-letter confirmation methodology, rendering it legally sufficient; (3) the 2024 Regional Transmission Plan identifies Import Path 2 as a “critical component” needed by 2030; (4) the Far West Import Generic Transmission Constraints announced in April 2026 independently validate need; and (5) intervenors offered only speculation that non-transmission alternatives could meet Permian Basin reliability needs. None of these arguments are persuasive on this record, and each is addressed below.
The Applicants’ Brief does not engage with the most damaging evidence in the record: that Oncor Vice President Collin Martin, P.E., acknowledged under cross-examination that “[t]he words on the page say that two of the three are needed” in 2030 — not Import Path 2; that 54 to 55 percent of the non-oil-and-gas load underlying the PBRP was confirmed only by TSP officer letters throughout the study; that ERCOT’s own Board-approved realization-rate methodology would reduce the projected 2030 total load from 23,659 MW to approximately 18,440 MW; that the ERCOT-commissioned Bureau of Economic Geology study projected oil-and-gas load reaching only 5,682 MW by 2035, compared to the Oncor-submitted S&P Global figure of 11,964 MW by 2030; and that the two largest planned data center complexes in the Permian Basin — Pacifico GW Ranch (7.65 GW) and Chevron (2.5–5 GW) — are each being built with their own gas-fired generation, specifically to avoid grid interconnection. 
The Commission should not approve a $13-to-$15-billion, multi-decade infrastructure commitment on a record containing this level of unaddressed uncertainty, particularly Import Path 2, which ERCOT has stated is not needed until 2038.

II. ARGUMENT
A.	ERCOT’s Recommendation Is Entitled to Great Weight but Does Not Eliminate the Commission’s Independent Obligation to Find Need on the Record.
The Applicants correctly note that 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii)(II) requires the Commission to give “great weight” to ERCOT’s recommendation that a reliability project is needed. But they overread that provision. “Great weight” in this case is a multiplier, it is not conclusive weight. If the original recommendation is flawed and has no weight or merit itself, 25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii)(II) does not automatically give credence where there is none originally. The Commission’s rules require it to evaluate ERCOT’s recommendation considering the evidentiary record developed in the contested-case proceeding, and the Commission’s own prior orders have recognized that need remains a contested issue to be resolved on the record on this CCN docket.
The burden of proof rests with the Applicants under PURA § 37.056(a), which authorizes a certificate only upon a showing that the proposed transmission facilities are necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public. Applicants must affirmatively demonstrate both (1) a specific, quantifiable need for the project and (2) how the proposed facilities will address that need. It is not the responsibility of landowner intervenors to disprove need. On this record, the Applicants have satisfied neither requirement.
The “great weight” standard also does not resolve the specific evidentiary deficiencies this brief identifies. ERCOT’s reliability recommendation was based on a load forecast that ERCOT’s own Board-approved realization-rate methodology would reduce by more than 20 percent, that the Texas Legislature has since identified as representing a stranded-infrastructure risk warranting additional scrutiny under Senate Bill 6, and that relies heavily on cryptocurrency mining at 58 to 59 percent of non-oil-and-gas load — a category that is by its nature is unusually mobile and volatile. If the underlying forecast cannot support the need finding, ERCOT’s recommendation based on it cannot supply that support either.
B.	Applicants Never Quantified the Alleged Need, and H.B. 5066 Did Not Relieve Them of That Burden.
The Application relies principally upon House Bill 5066 and ERCOT’s Permian Basin Reliability Plan (“PBRP”) to establish project need. The Applicants argue that the use of TSP officer letters to confirm load was “mandated by H.B. 5066” and is therefore unassailable. This misstates the statutory structure. House Bill 5066 amended PURA § 37.056(c)(2) to require the Commission to “consider” loads seeking interconnection without a signed agreement; it did not require the Commission to treat those loads as proven or to accept them uncritically as a sufficient basis for need. 
More fundamentally, neither the PBRP nor HB 5066 identifies a specific, quantifiable transmission deficiency that this project is designed to remedy. The PBRP contains forecasts of future load growth but does not identify the amount of available generation or transmission capacity that will exist at the time those loads materialize. Without identifying available supply, neither ERCOT nor the Applicants can determine the actual magnitude of any deficit requiring correction. As a result, the record contains no establishment of evidence:
the number of megawatts of import capability allegedly required at Big Hill;
the number of megawatts allegedly required at Sand Lake;
the amount of transmission capability necessary to address any identified deficit; or
the amount of power this specific transmission line is expected to deliver.
The absence of these basic engineering and planning metrics prevents meaningful evaluation of whether the proposed project is appropriately sized, reasonably necessary, or capable of addressing the claimed reliability concerns. The Application does not identify the anticipated transfer level for Import Path 2, does not compare alternative voltage levels or configurations, and does not evaluate less costly or smaller-scale alternatives.
Even the Applicants’ own brief acknowledges that ERCOT’s 2025 adjusted load-forecast methodology — approved by the ERCOT Board in April 2025 — applies a 55.4 percent realization rate to officer-letter-confirmed load and reduces data center load projections to approximately 27.6 percent of their original value. That system-wide comparison is beside the point. The question is whether the Permian Basin-specific load — the load that actually justifies these import paths — remains sufficient after applying the same discount. The Applicants do not apply the 55.4 percent realization rate to the 11,695 MW Permian-specific non-oil-and-gas figure shown in their own Table 1, do not apply the 27.6 percent data center discount to the data center component of it, and offer no analysis of whether the 765-kV import paths remain necessary at the resulting reduced load level. 
The statutory authorization to consider officer-letter loads in planning does not relieve the Applicants of their burden to demonstrate, on this evidentiary record, that the load those letters describe is sufficiently durable to support a multi-decade, $4-to-$5-billion infrastructure commitment in Import Path 2.  Also, the Applicants did not establish, through record evidence, that projected load requiring transmission service excludes load expected to be served by behind-the-meter or self-supplied generation.  They rely heavily on ERCOT's forecasts while not demonstrating how those forecasts accounted for large loads that intend to self-supply. The Applicants do not identify whether projected load was reduced to reflect known or anticipated self-generation.  If the projected transmission load is overstated because it includes demand that will not rely on the ERCOT transmission system, then the Commission should carefully evaluate whether the applicants have met their burden of demonstrating the extent of transmission facilities that are "necessary."  
Applicants repeatedly rely on ERCOT's load forecast as proof of need, yet they identify no testimony demonstrating how the forecast distinguishes between projected electrical demand and projected demand requiring transmission service from the ERCOT grid. Without that showing, the Commission cannot simply assume every announced large load will require the level of bulk transmission proposed.
C.	Applicants Failed to Demonstrate That Bell County East Can Supply the Power Allegedly Required.
Even assuming a future deficit exists in the Permian Basin, the Applicants failed to demonstrate that sufficient power is available at Bell County East to serve Import Path 2. ERCOT planning documents identify reliability concerns and supply constraints within the Central Texas Corridor, including the Bell County area, in their 2023-RTP, 2024-RTP and 2025-RTP:
ERCOT’s 2025-RTP note, “Similar to the 2023 and 2024 RTPs, the 2025 RTP assessment results highlighted the ongoing need for major import pathway enhancements to the Central Texas corridor.” 
ERCOT has identified the need for additional transmission to import approximately 2,000 MW into Central Texas, in their 2025-RTP. 
Applicants provided no evidence reconciling this constraint with their claim that Bell County East can serve as a major export source for Import Path 2.
Applicants did not identify generation resources expected to supply Import Path 2.
Applicants did not quantify expected power flows on the proposed line.
Without evidence of surplus available generation at the source end of the line, the Applicants have failed to show the project can perform its asserted function. A 765-kV line authorized to transmit bulk power into the Permian Basin is of no reliability value if the generation to fill it has not been identified and cannot be exported from the source region.
D.	The Load Forecast Underlying the Claimed Need Has Not Been Shown Reliable.
The claimed need for Import Path 2 rests on load forecasts that have not been shown to be reliable, validated, or consistent with subsequent ERCOT planning developments. The record reflects multiple, compounding deficiencies.
1.	Officer-Letter Load Remains Unvalidated.
In the PBRP study process, within three months the forecasted non-oil-and-gas load of 11,995 MW was changed from 54% unconfirmed to 6% unconfirmed; the 6% confirmed by TSP officer letters was changed to 55%.  How did that happen?  The confirmed by contract remained the same with 38%, but only 4,558 MW out of the total 11,995 MW.  
Specifically:
In March 2024, approximately 38 percent of additional non-oil-and-gas load was supported by binding contracts; approximately 54 percent was unconfirmed; and approximately 6 percent confirmed TSP Officer letters.
By June 2024, approximately 55 percent of forecasted load was now supported by TSP officer letters and 6 percent was unconfirmed.
2.	Cryptocurrency Mining Load Is Unusually Volatile.
Cryptocurrency mining comprised approximately 58–59 percent of forecasted non-oil-and-gas load, 6,900 MW.  The cryptocurrency sector has continued to experience consolidation, bankruptcies, asset sales, and shifts toward alternative business models, making it an uncertain foundation for long-term transmission planning.
ERCOT documented 26 events since 2023 in which data centers and cryptocurrency mining load tripped offline during normal voltage disturbances, creating cascading outage risks.
ERCOT’s Board designated the proposed fix as a Priority Revision Request.
The Texas Legislature enacted Senate Bill 6 specifically to reduce reliance on speculative large-load interconnection requests of the type that drove the PBRP forecast.  It is based on a load the Legislature has since identified as a stranded infrastructure risk
3.	ERCOT’s Realization-Rate Methodology Was Never Applied to the Permian-Specific Forecast.
ERCOT adopted a more conservative adjusted load-forecast methodology using realization rates, approved by the ERCOT Board in April 2025. The Applicants did not show the Permian Basin-specific forecast was updated or validated under this methodology, and they did not reconcile the PBRP forecast with the Bureau of Economic Geology study, which projected oil-and-gas-related load reaching only 5,682 MW by 2035 — compared to the Oncor-submitted S&P Global figure of 11,964 MW by 2030.
PBRP adopted the industry-submitted number and did not reconcile or even acknowledge the independently commissioned academic study. Because the claimed need depends entirely on future load assumptions that are unvalidated and outdated, the forecast does not constitute substantial evidence of need.
E.	The 2024 RTP Does Not Establish That Import Path 2 Is Needed in 2030 — and Oncor’s Own Vice President Conceded as Much.
The Applicants’ principal evidence that Import Path 2 is needed in 2030 rests almost entirely on the title of one figure: Figure 18 of the 2024 RTP, labeled “The 765-kV Core Plan needed in 2030.”,  but the body text of the 2024 RTP on the preceding page states that the three Permian Basin 765-kV import paths were “incorporated into the start case” for the study — not that they were independently determined to be needed in 2030.  A mislabeled figure title cannot override the plain meaning of the body text.
This reading is confirmed by ERCOT’s own December 12, 2024 Sequencing Letter to the Commissioners, which identified only two of the three import paths as needed in 2030 and left Import Path 2 in the 2038 timeframe. And it is confirmed by Oncor’s own Vice President, Collin Martin, who — after initially resisting the question on June 9, 2026 — acknowledged under direct questioning on June 10, 2026, that “[t]he words on the page say that two of the three are needed.” The Commission should not make a $4-billion, 400-mile decision on a misleading figure label when the body text, the Sequencing Letter, and the Applicants’ own lead witness all point the other direction.
The Applicants’ own filings compound this problem. Issue 19 of the Applicants’ Brief states that “[t]he Project is expected to be in-service by December 2030.”  If Import Path 2 were truly needed in 2030 — as the Applicants argue from the label on Figure 18 — a December 2030 in-service date would leave no operational margin. A transmission project of this scale requires years of construction after CCN approval; there is no realistic scenario in which a line approved in September 2026 is built, energized, and serving load by December 2030. That internal inconsistency is itself evidence that the 2038 sequencing in the PBRP — not the 2030 label derived from a figure title — reflects ERCOT’s actual determination of when Import Path 2 is needed, which is irrefutably 2038.
F.	The April 2026 Far West GTCs Do Not Cure the Evidentiary Deficiencies in the Load Forecast.
The Applicants introduce ERCOT’s April 2026 declaration that the 765-kV import paths are needed to resolve the newly announced North-to-Far-West and South-to-Far-West Import Generic Transmission Constraints by 2030. This evidence was introduced on rebuttal, after the close of direct testimony, and it raises a threshold question the Applicants do not answer: if the Far West Import GTCs independently validate need for Import Path 2 by 2030, why did ERCOT not identify them in the PBRP itself — the document the Applicants rely on as their “sole basis for need”? The emergence of new GTCs in April 2026 — more than 18 months after the PBRP was completed — suggests changed conditions, not validation of the original forecast.
The GTC evidence also does not address the core evidentiary problem: whether the load the Project would serve is durable enough to justify construction. GTCs measure transmission system constraints; they do not validate the composition or reliability of the load on the demand side. A GTC driven substantially by speculative cryptocurrency mining load that may not materialize is not the same as a GTC driven by stable industrial or residential load. The Applicants do not disaggregate the load driving the GTC constraint from the speculative load that undermines the PBRP forecast.
G.	The Record Contains Specific, Named, Verified Evidence of Alternatives — Not Speculation.
The Applicants characterize all intervenor evidence on alternatives as “speculation.” That characterization cannot be squared with the specific, named, sourced evidence in the record. Ms. Graci’s Exhibit A identifies thirty-seven planned or announced natural gas generation projects in the Permian Basin, West Texas, and Panhandle/Northwest regions totaling approximately 39.467 gigawatts of new capacity. This is not speculation; it is publicly available project-tracking data identifying specific projects by name, county, and capacity.
This week Governor Greg Abbott announced the eighth Texas Energy Fund (TxEF) loan for 860 megawatts (MW) of new, reliable power in Ward County. Vistra’s project consists of two new natural gas units at its Permian Basin Power Plant, more than tripling the site’s current capacity.
The Texas Energy Fund, which is administered by the Commission, also awarded a loan to Competitive Power Ventures[A] for a 1,350 megawatt (MW) natural gas, combined cycle, and generation facility at CPV’s Basin Ranch Energy Center in Ward County.  It’s expected to begin generating power in 2029 and will interconnect in the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) West Load Zone.
[A] https://www.gem.wiki/CPV_Basin_Ranch_Energy_Center
Nor is the off-grid evidence speculative. Two of the largest planned Permian Basin data center complexes — Pacifico Energy’s GW Ranch (7.65 GW, permitted by TCEQ as the largest air pollution permit ever issued in Texas), and Chevron’s Reeves County data center (2.5 to 5 GW, announced November 2025) — are each being built with their own gas-fired generation and no grid interconnection. These are not intervenor projections; they are announced projects with TCEQ permits, SEC filings, and press releases in the public record.
ERCOT itself acknowledged in its PBRP reliability study that the “lack of conventional generation in the Permian Basin region” is the driving factor for the 765-kV import paths. Yet the record shows that conventional generation is actively being developed in the Permian Basin at a scale that rivals or exceeds the PBRP’s projected load — and that the largest loads are choosing to self-provision, specifically to avoid the transmission grid.
The Texas Legislature directed ERCOT to solve a Permian reliability problem, and the private sector is now helping to solve it faster, cheaper, and without eminent domain, through behind-the-meter gas generation at the source.
The Applicants were exempted from any formal alternatives analysis by virtue of the project’s reliability-project designation; however, the Commission should not close the door to that analysis now.
H.	The Applicants’ Own Table Confirms the Oil-and-Gas Load Discrepancy.
The Applicants’ Brief presents a table showing that the PBRP incorporated oil-and-gas load of 11,964 MW in 2030 and 14,705 MW in 2038. Applicants’ Br. at 35 (Table 1). This is the S&P Global forecast that ERCOT’s own Permian Basin Reliability Plan Study confirms was “developed by S&P Global and submitted to ERCOT by Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC.”  The Applicants do not address the independent academic study ERCOT itself commissioned from the Bureau of Economic Geology at the University of Texas at Austin, which projected oil-and-gas-related load reaching only 5,682 MW by 2035 in its base case — compared to the 11,964 MW Oncor-submitted figure for five years earlier. The PBRP adopted the industry-submitted number and did not reconcile or even acknowledge the independently commissioned academic study. The Applicants’ Reply Brief offers no explanation for that omission.

III. CONCLUSION AND PRAYER FOR RELIEF
The Applicants’ Initial Brief does not rebut the specific evidentiary record on which Judy Graci’s need to challenge rests. The “great weight” standard does not eliminate the Commission’s independent obligation to find need; the Applicants failed to quantify the alleged deficit or identify available generation to fill the proposed line; HB 5066 did not eliminate the evidentiary bar; the 2024 RTP — on its own body text and by the Applicants’ Collin Martin, Vice President’s admission — does not establish that Import Path 2 is needed in 2030; the April 2026 GTCs do not validate the reliability of the underlying load; and the alternatives evidence in the record is specific and sourced, not speculative.
For the foregoing reasons and those stated in Judy Graci’s Initial Brief, she respectfully requests that the Administrative Law Judges find that the Applicants have not carried their burden to prove public convenience and necessity for the Project and recommend that the Commission deny the requested certificate of convenience and necessity.

Respectfully submitted,
